Gradually integrating new technologies allows for implementing controlled transitions, testing innovations in real- world settings, and ensuring that they meet the military’s requirements before full-scale adoption. Due to the rapid evolution of technologies, DOW might want to exercise extra caution before entering multi-decadal contracts, power purchase agreements, and leases. It would be wise to evaluate whether the market will evolve, or technology might become obsolete (i.e., superseded by superior new technology) during the contract period. Budgets could include a shorter replacement period for such systems, or contracts could include early termination terms advantageous to the government, or, in the case of energy performance contracts, the contract requirements could put the risk of change onto the other party. Budgets should also plan for charging infrastructure, cybersecurity, local electricity prices, and requirements for battery disposal or recycling (Tegler 2025). 6.12 Repurposing Infrastructure Repurposing legacy infrastructure could present a cost-effective way to integrate advanced energy technologies (EPA 2020). Out-of-service generation assets can be repurposed for biogas, biomass, or other advanced energy projects, reducing installation costs by $45 to $113 per kilowatt hour (EPA 2020). Biogas can be transported via existing pipelines to facilities where the gas can be used directly or processed into natural gas (Raythatha and Olsen 2024). Additionally, oil and gas wells can be used to harness geothermal energy through retrofitting inactive wells or co-production on active wells (DOE GTO 2025). Black-start Black-start capability refers to the ability of a power system or specific capability generating units to restart and restore power without relying on an external power grid. From an inertial perspective, black start involves initiating the system recovery in the absence of grid-supplied frequency and voltage references, which are normally stabilized by the inertia of synchronized rotating machines (for more information on inertia, see Gracia et al. [2019]). In conventional systems, the inertia provided by large synchronous generators helps maintain grid stability during fluctuations. During black-start situations, this inertial support is initially absent, requiring black-start units to independently establish the system frequency and voltage.
